---
title: "Quickstart"
description: "Install oboro, wire the Claude Code hooks in, and clean and restore a document by hand for everything else."
---

## Install

Pick whichever fits; the install script is the quickest.

### Install script

Downloads the prebuilt binary for macOS or Linux and verifies it against the release checksums:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://m.canouil.dev/oboro/install.sh | bash
```

It installs into `/usr/local/bin` when writable, otherwise `~/.local/bin`.
Pin a version with `--version`, choose a directory with `--dir`, and pass `--help` for the rest.
The script needs `bash` and `curl`; on a minimal distribution such as Alpine, install them first with `apk add bash curl`.

To also find names nobody told the tool about, install the ner build and fetch its model:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://m.canouil.dev/oboro/install.sh | bash -s -- --features ner
oboro models pull   # about 348 MB, once
```

On Linux the ner binary needs glibc 2.39 or newer (Ubuntu 24.04+, Debian 13+); the default binary is static and runs anywhere.

### Docker

No toolchain needed; the image is one static binary on `distroless`.
The vault volume is not optional, because the placeholder mapping lives in it:

```bash
docker volume create oboro-vault
docker run --rm \
  -v oboro-vault:/vault \
  -v "$PWD":/work -w /work \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  ghcr.io/mcanouil/oboro:latest clean contract.docx
```

The [Docker](docker.qmd) page covers `restore` and the volume in full, along with the `ghcr.io/mcanouil/oboro:ner` variant, which finds untold names with the recognition model already inside the image.

### Prebuilt binary, by hand

Download the archive for your machine and `SHA256SUMS` from the [releases page](https://github.com/mcanouil/oboro/releases), then verify and install it:

```bash
VERSION=0.1.0
TARGET=x86_64-unknown-linux-musl   # or the row that matches your machine

curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/mcanouil/oboro/releases/download/${VERSION}/oboro-${VERSION}-${TARGET}.tar.gz"
curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/mcanouil/oboro/releases/download/${VERSION}/SHA256SUMS"
sha256sum --ignore-missing --check SHA256SUMS   # shasum -a 256 on macOS
tar -xzf "oboro-${VERSION}-${TARGET}.tar.gz"
install -m 0755 oboro /usr/local/bin/oboro
```

### With Rust already installed

```bash
cargo install --git https://github.com/mcanouil/oboro
```

### From source

Required for `ocr`, which no prebuilt binary or image carries, and for a `ner` build on a Linux distribution older than the prebuilt one's glibc:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/mcanouil/oboro.git
cd oboro
cargo build --release
```

The binary lands in `target/release/oboro`.

That plain build depends on nothing but Rust.
Two capabilities are optional: reading images needs the Tesseract system libraries, and recognising names links ONNX Runtime, which the build fetches over the network.
The ner build is also shipped prebuilt, by the [install script](#install-script) and as [a Docker image](docker.qmd); ocr is compiled in rather than shipped.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Names and companies

Finding names nobody told the tool about needs the recognition model:

```bash
cargo build --release --features ner   # downloads ONNX Runtime while building
oboro models pull
```

The build downloads ONNX Runtime, so `--features ner` needs network access and a fully offline build fails here.
`models pull` then fetches the model, about 348 MB once, checked against pinned hashes.
Once built, it is the only command that touches the network.

## Images

Reading images and scanned documents needs Tesseract, plus trained data for the languages your documents are in:

```bash
# Debian and Ubuntu; add a tesseract-ocr-<language> package per language
sudo apt-get install tesseract-ocr tesseract-ocr-eng libtesseract-dev libleptonica-dev

# macOS; tesseract-lang installs the trained data for every language
brew install tesseract tesseract-lang

cargo build --release --features ocr
```

Whatever is installed is used, so no language has to be declared.
Set [`ocr_languages`](configuration.qmd#ocr_languages) to pick among them.

## Both

```bash
cargo build --release --features "ner,ocr"
```

:::

### In a devcontainer

For building or contributing with nothing on the host but Docker.
The container carries the pinned Rust toolchain, Tesseract and the OCR libraries, so `cargo build --release --features "ner,ocr"` runs inside it without setting up a host toolchain, and the binary lands in `target/release/oboro` as usual.
In Visual Studio Code or a GitHub Codespace, reopen the folder in the container when prompted; [Development](development.qmd) has the manual `docker` invocation.

Check what your build can do:

```bash
oboro doctor
```

## Wire it into Claude Code

Do this first if you use Claude Code.
The agent reads files itself, so cleaning a copy by hand and pasting it in protects nothing: it already read the original.

Two hooks put Oboro in that path.
The plugin names them both and brings the skill that explains their placeholders:

```text
/plugin marketplace add mcanouil/oboro
/plugin install oboro@oboro
```

The plugin cannot install the binary its hooks run, so install that first, with any of the ways above.
Without one, every matching tool result is withheld and every matching write is refused, and the message says what to install: the plugin fails closed rather than leaving you unprotected while looking installed.

If you would rather keep the hooks in your own settings, one command names them both instead:

```bash
oboro hook install
```

It asks whether to cover this project or every project, and shows what it will write before writing it.
Pass `--project` or `--user` to skip the question, and `--dry-run` to see the settings without writing them.

This is what it adds, next to whatever your settings already hold:

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Read|Grep|Bash|WebFetch",
        "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "oboro hook post-tool-use" }]
      }
    ],
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Write|Edit",
        "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "oboro hook pre-tool-use" }]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Nothing already in the file is moved, reordered or removed, and a hook Oboro finds already named is left exactly as you wrote it.
Write it by hand instead if you would rather: the command is a convenience, not the only way in.

Then check it took:

```bash
oboro doctor
```

```text
PostToolUse .claude/settings.local.json (Read|Grep|Bash|WebFetch, reachable)
PreToolUse  .claude/settings.local.json (Write|Edit, reachable)
```

Installed as a plugin, the hooks are in the plugin's own files rather than in your settings, and `doctor` says so:

```text
plugin      /home/you/.claude/settings.json (oboro@oboro, enabled)
PostToolUse not in your settings; the plugin carries it
PreToolUse  not in your settings; the plugin carries it
```

Ask the agent to read a file holding a phone number, and it will tell you about `[[PHONE_1]]`.
Ask it to write that back, and the real number lands in the file.

Install both halves, which is what `oboro hook install` does.
The first without the second means the model is shown placeholders and nothing puts them back, so `[[PHONE_1]]` ends up in your source.

`reachable` is worth reading: a hook naming a binary that is not on `PATH` is configured and useless, and it fails closed on every matching tool call.

At 17 to 70 ms a call this runs on every matching tool without being felt; the [timings](how-it-works.qmd#what-a-run-costs) are recorded.
The [reference](reference.qmd#hook) covers what each half does, and what neither covers.

::: {.callout-warning}

## Your own words are not covered

The hooks clean what tools read and write.
What you type into the chat is never touched, because the event that fires on a prompt can add context to it but cannot rewrite it.

Paste a document rather than retyping what is in it, and the hook covers it.

:::

## Tell the agent what it is reading

With the hooks on, the agent reads `[[PHONE_1]]` without being told what that is.
Left to guess, it reads a placeholder as a bug in your file, as a template to fill in, or as a redaction to work around.

The plugin above already carries it, so this section is for anyone who did not install that way; installing it twice is not worth doing.

Install the skill that explains them:

```bash
oboro skill install
```

It asks whether to install for this project or for every project, and names the file it will write before writing it:

```text
1  this project    /home/you/project/.claude/skills/oboro/SKILL.md
2  every project   /home/you/.claude/skills/oboro/SKILL.md
Install the Oboro skill where? [1/2]
```

Pass `--project` or `--user` to skip the question.
`oboro skill show` prints the text without writing anything.

Then check it took, as with the hooks:

```bash
oboro doctor
```

```text
skill       /home/you/project/.claude/skills/oboro/SKILL.md (current)
skill       /home/you/.claude/skills/oboro/SKILL.md (not installed)
```

The skill is carried in the binary, so it describes the version of the hooks you have rather than the ones documented when you installed.
Edit the installed copy and a later install leaves your edit alone, writing what it would have installed to `SKILL.md.oboro-proposed` beside it.

For an agent other than Claude Code, the same skill is one command away:

```bash
npx skills add mcanouil/oboro
```

That reads `skills/oboro/SKILL.md` from this repository and installs it for whichever agents it finds.
It installs the explanation and not the machine: no binary, no hooks, and nothing redacted until you add both.
It also symlinks the skill by default, and Oboro does not write through a symbolic link, so `oboro skill install` afterwards names the link and refuses rather than overwriting what you installed.

## Clean a document

Everything below is the manual loop.
It is the primary path in any tool without hooks, and the fallback in Claude Code for a document you would rather handle yourself.

```bash
oboro clean contract.docx
```

That writes `contract.clean.md` beside the input and tells you what it replaced:

```text
contract.docx -> contract.clean.md (7 replaced: ADDRESS 2, EMAIL 1, IBAN 1, ORG 1, PERSON 1, PHONE 1)
```

Read it, then paste it into whichever model you are using.

Point `clean` at a directory to do a whole folder at once; add `--recursive` to include its subfolders:

```bash
oboro clean contracts/ --recursive
```

## Decide for yourself what gets hidden

`clean` redacts everything it finds.
`review` shows you the list first and lets you reject anything it got wrong:

```bash
oboro review contract.docx
```

```text
┌ contract.docx  —  6 of 7 will be redacted ─────────────────────┐
│ [x] PERSON      31%  Jean Dupont                               │
│ [x] ORG         52%  Acme Consulting SARL                      │
│ [ ] PERSON      22%  Le Havre                                  │
│ [x] IBAN       100%  FR14 2004 1010 0505 0001 3M02 606         │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
 j/k move   space toggle   a accept all   n reject none   w write
```

Rejecting a detection leaves the value in the output and never records it anywhere.

## Bring the answer back

The model replies using the placeholders.
Save its answer and put the real values back:

```bash
oboro restore answer.md
```

Or keep it in a pipeline:

```bash
pbpaste | oboro restore
```

## A whole round trip

```bash
oboro clean contract.docx --stdout | pbcopy   # paste into the model
pbpaste | oboro restore                       # read what it said, with real values
```
